abstract: This study uses newly released Facebook engagement data covering millions of shared web links to examine how different categories of news are viewed and shared by various types of U.S. users. The authors distinguish among low-credibility news publishers, credible news sources, clickbait purveyors, and political news, using curated lists and supervised classifiers. The findings describe patterns in the distribution and consumption of these news types across user demographics on the platform.
key_claims: Different categories of news (low-credibility, credible, clickbait, and political) circulate on Facebook in distinguishable, category-specific patterns.
Newly available platform engagement data can reveal how news is seen and shared across categories of U.S. users, offering a large-scale empirical view previously unavailable.
The results corroborate recent findings in the study of online news exposure and sharing (as suggested by the abstract's reference to supporting prior work).
methods: Analysis of newly available Facebook engagement data covering millions of shared web links.
Classification of articles into categories: low-credibility publishers, credible news sources, clickbait, and political news.
Combination of curated source lists with supervised machine-learning classifiers to identify article categories.
Description of viewing and sharing behavior segmented by categories of U.S. users.
findings: The paper reports patterns in how and by which user categories different news types are seen and shared on Facebook (specific results not available from the abstract alone).
Findings are stated to support recent research in the area, though the abstract is truncated and specific results are not fully specified.
contributions: First-of-its-kind analysis of the newly released, large-scale Facebook link engagement dataset.
A framework combining curated lists and supervised classifiers to categorize news by credibility, clickbait status, and political content.
Empirical description of how news exposure and sharing vary across U.S. user categories on a major social platform.
framing: The paper is situated within research on misinformation, news consumption, and political communication on social media, contributing to debates about how low-credibility and political content spreads on platforms like Facebook.
